newsitem.title: USA: Fla tobacco suit complicated by workers comp issue.
newsitem.headline: Fla tobacco suit complicated by workers comp issue.

text.p: Selecting a jury in a landmark secondhand-smoke lawsuit has been complicated by the fact that many potential jurors believe tobacco companies are not the proper targets of the suit, attorneys said on Thursday.

Instead, many of those questioned by lawyers say the flight attendants represented in the class action should have targeted their employers -- the airlines -- in seeking damages for illnesses allegedly caused by breathing cigarette smoke during flights.

By midmorning Thursday, the 11th day of jury selection, attorneys had assembled only 63 members of the pool from which the final panel of six jurors and 10 alternates will be selected. The pool eventually is expected to have about 100 people.
Ninety percent of the latest group of potential jurors to be called said they felt flight attendants should have targeted their airlines, Susan Rosenblatt, an attorney for the plaintiffs, said.

The suit, known as Norma Broin vs Philip Morris Cos Inc, was filed on behalf of thousands of non-smoking flight attendants seeking as much as $5 billion in damages from tobacco companies for illnesses they attribute to breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

Rosenblatt asked the court to inform jurors that workers compensation law prohibited the flight attendants from filing such a lawsuit against their employers. The plaintiffs believe that jurors who feel they should not be suing likely would not be able to be impartial.

But Circuit Judge Robert Kaye declined to do so without granting the tobacco attorneys' request that he tell jurors that the flight attendants could obtain some relief by making workers compensation claims. Rosenblatt opposed that request.
In that case, Kaye said, "We will just proceed as we have been proceeding."
The trial is expected to take up to three months after jury selection is completed.
